name: Maya Nakamura

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks for making time. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. Tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm doing law, and so far it's three lectures a day, a seminar on Thursdays and a lot of reading in the library with a flask of tea. I take handwritten notes in a blue notebook because I think better on paper. Two evenings and Sunday mornings I work at a second-hand bookshop on Fenner Road.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: And how does money work for you right now, between family, the part-time job and the course?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Mum is a nurse and Dad drives a bus, and together they cover my share of the rent in the flat I split with three others. I cover food and books from the bookshop wage, about 90 a week. I got a small scholarship for my results, which is why I could say yes to this university at all.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Here is the first picture, called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, it was always going to be a lot of noise. At the bookshop my manager Paula already reads three articles a week saying robots will take everything, and I'd tell her to relax. Online I'd probably post a joke about all the money that was wasted.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly it doesn't mean much for me, which is a relief. I still have loans coming, and I'm not sure a law degree guarantees a training contract even when nothing changes. Law is competitive, and the vacation scheme places are tiny.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep going exactly as now: lectures, bookshop shifts, saving 20 a week. I'd apply for a vacation scheme in my second year and join the law society. I wouldn't change course, because there's nothing to react to.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm-ish, though not fully. It's relief mixed with the normal fear that rent goes up and my parents can't keep helping. It's a bit boring to feel safe about the wrong thing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd shrug. What would still weigh on you if nothing changes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Rent and debt, mostly. If rent goes up by 40 a month, my mum picks up extra shifts, and I hate that. That's the thing I'd lose sleep over, not any machine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which of those would you tell your parents about, and which would you keep to yourself?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my parents about the vacation scheme because they love hearing that. The money worry I'd keep to myself. My dad already skips lunch some days, and I don't want to add to it by sounding scared.

say: I'd tell my manager Paula that **hype** always burns out and she can stop worrying.
Online I'd joke that the money wasted on this stuff could have funded a **library**.
think: Privately I still worry about **rent** rising and my parents picking up extra shifts.
I doubt a law degree guarantees a **training contract**, whatever AI does.
do: Keep working Sunday shifts at the **bookshop** and saving 20 a week.
Apply for a law vacation scheme in second year and join the **law society**.
feel: Relieved on AI, but still tight about **money** at home.
S0.quote: My dad already skips lunch some days, and I don't want to add to it by sounding scared.
fieldNote: Her worry is **money at home**, not machines, and she shields her parents from it.
She calls the AI talk noise, which fits her distrust of the industry.
Said very little about changing course; the plan is the ordinary legal route.

steps.text: Keep the Sunday and two weekday evening shifts at the bookshop
Put 20 a week into a savings account for rent

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Next picture, called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where we need rules. If software starts doing legal research and contract checking, the firms will hire fewer juniors and call it progress. I'd go to the student union meeting and push for a motion asking the university to say what it's doing about it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think paralegal and trainee work is exactly what gets shrunk, because it's reading and checking. I don't use these tools and I don't want to, but I'm scared that's become a disadvantage. If other applicants can do twice the work with them, I lose by being principled.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Over the first year I'd join the union branch for students and the law society's campaign group. I'd still keep my notes by hand, but I'd sit in on one workshop on how the tools are used in firms so I can argue against them knowing what they do. I'd also look for work experience at a legal aid centre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I feel like I'm being asked to run a race while someone moves the finish line. I don't mind hard work, but I mind not knowing what the work is.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said the junior legal jobs worry you. Who would you worry about most?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly the girls and boys in my seminar group who go into firms as trainees. Hamza (a classmate) already says he wants a firm job and his family is counting on it. If those places shrink, people with no safety net go first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you say to your mum and dad about the degree, if it came to that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my mum and dad the degree is still worth it, and I'd mean it. But I'd also say I might look at legal aid or the public sector instead. Nobody I know in nursing is told a robot will do their shift.

say: I'd push the student union to ask the university what it is doing about **graduate jobs**.
I'd say firms use AI as an excuse to hire fewer **juniors**.
think: Reading and checking are exactly the **trainee tasks** that shrink first.
Being principled and not using the tools may leave me **behind** other applicants.
do: Join the student union branch and the law society's **campaign group** this term.
Look for work experience at a **legal aid** centre instead of a big firm.
feel: **Anxious**, like the finish line is moving while I run.
S1.quote: I feel like I'm being asked to run a race while someone moves the finish line. I don't mind hard work, but I mind not knowing what the work is.
fieldNote: Her answer turns toward **collective action** and rules rather than personal tool use.
She admits her refusal to use AI could cost her, which is a real tension.
Named a classmate, Hamza, whose family has the most riding on a firm job.

steps.text: Join the student union branch and attend the next motion meeting
Write to the law faculty asking how graduate hiring will change
Volunteer one afternoon a week at a legal aid centre

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it out loud, to anyone: this is a decision, not weather. Governments let a few companies run this and nobody voted for it. I'd post it, I'd go to a march, I'd say it at the bookshop even to customers who just want a paperback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I think my degree might be worth far less than what my parents are paying toward it. By the time I finish, which is 2029, the thinking jobs I'm training for may belong to software. That's an awful thing to say to my mum, who works nights to help me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start organising immediately, with the union and other students, because in two years no one can wait. I'd push the university to let students pause fees. I'd keep my scholarship by passing exams, and I'd try to find a practical skill, maybe through a hospital volunteering placement, that doesn't depend on a screen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed. I can't sleep on this one. It's not just me, it's my whole family, because Mum and Dad's jobs are hands-on but my degree isn't.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Two years is very short. What changes for you compared with the slower versions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The big difference is time. With two years there's no chance to retrain slowly or even finish the degree. I'd feel I have to act now and loudly, because nobody else in charge will.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who is responsible, in your view, if it comes that fast?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The companies, first, and the governments that let them run ahead. I wouldn't blame the engineers so much as the people who treat the whole thing as a race. I'd tell them directly that a decision this big can't be made by ten firms.

say: I'd say loudly that a few firms and **governments** made this decision and nobody voted.
I'd go to a **march** and talk about it even at the bookshop till.
think: My degree could be worth far less than what my parents pay by **2029**.
I feel guilty telling **mum** this while she works night shifts to help.
do: Organise with the student **union** to demand fee pauses and public support.
Volunteer at a **hospital** to try a hands-on path that doesn't depend on screens.
feel: **Alarmed**, with sleepless nights, because the whole family depends on my degree paying off.
S2.quote: Governments let a few companies run this and nobody voted for it.
fieldNote: She shifts to **anger** at firms and governments, not at the technology itself.
Two years removes her slow options, so she turns to loud organising.
The sharpest worry is guilt about her mother, a night-shift nurse.

steps.text: Organise a student union petition asking for a fee pause
Go to a march and write to my local politician
Try a hospital volunteering placement for a hands-on option
Ask the scholarship office what happens if the course ends early

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Now the picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's winnable if we act. Five years is enough to pass laws, build unions and change what universities teach. I'd say the same things as before but with a plan: a petition, a campus meeting, a letter to our local MP every term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'm still scared, but I can see how to finish the degree and perhaps get a job before it hits. I think the first jobs to go are mine, trainee and clerk jobs, but my parents' jobs last longer. That feels unfair, and also a little lucky.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the first two years, then pick modules in public law, employment law and human rights, because those are where rules get written. I'd apply for placements at a union legal team or an advice centre. I'd save 30 a week from the bookshop and avoid borrowing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious again, but steadier. Five years is long enough to feel I'm doing something.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Five years gives you some room. What would you use it for?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: With two years I'm panicking and swinging at everything. With five I can build something slowly, like a campaign group, and argue for rules.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How is this different from two years, in your own head?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd use it on the law and on my own savings. My plan is to finish the degree with no extra debt and then work wherever the rules are being written. If that doesn't exist, I'll help create it.

say: I'd say five years is **enough** to pass laws and change what universities teach.
I'd start a campus **petition** and write to our MP every term.
think: My trainee and **clerk** type jobs go first, while my parents' hands-on work lasts longer.
That feels unfair, and also a little **lucky**.
do: Pick **employment law** and public law modules where rules about AI get written.
Apply for a placement at a **union** legal team or advice centre.
feel: Still **anxious**, but steadier because there's time to build something.
S3.quote: With two years I'm panicking and swinging at everything. With five I can build something slowly, like a campaign group, and argue for rules.
fieldNote: More **structured** than the 2028 answer; time lets her turn anger into a plan.
She recognises her parents' hands-on jobs will outlast her own path.
Ties her degree choices directly to where rules get written.

steps.text: Start a campus petition on graduate jobs and rules for AI
Choose employment law and public law modules for second year
Save 30 a week from the bookshop and take no extra loan

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Last picture, called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a gift, and I'd say we need to use it before the money and power get fixed in place. I'd talk to friends about it as a fairness problem, not a technology one. The sooner the rules are in, the less people suffer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I feel almost calm. I'd be 28 and mid-career, with a law job and maybe a union role. My worry would be less about me and more about my mum, who'll be near retirement and depends on a pension.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep studying law, aim for a training contract, and join the union reps early. I'd also learn how these tools work, at last, in a controlled way, so I can argue against bad uses. I'd save into a pension from my first job, even small amounts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly. Ten years away feels a bit like knowing a storm is coming a long way off. You still check the roof, but you don't panic.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Ten years feels like plenty of time to some people. Does it to you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I'd still worry that nothing gets done until it's too late, because ten years sounds distant. People put it off, including me. I'd want the union and rules in place, and a system that helps older workers like my mum.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you want to have in place by then?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A decent pension for my mum and dad, a public fund that helps people move jobs, and rules that make firms explain what machines decide. If those exist, my own career feels fine whatever happens.

say: I'd say ten years is a **gift**, and we must use it for rules and fairness.
I'd frame it to friends as a **fairness** problem, not a technology one.
think: I feel almost calm about my own future, but I worry about **mum's** pension.
People will put it off because **ten years** sounds distant, and I might too.
do: Aim for a **training contract** and become a union rep early.
Finally learn how the tools work, in a **controlled** way, to argue against bad uses.
feel: Mostly **calm**, like seeing a storm far off and still checking the roof.
S4.quote: Ten years away feels a bit like knowing a storm is coming a long way off. You still check the roof, but you don't panic.
fieldNote: The first scenario where she admits she might **learn the tools**, but only to argue against them.
Her concern moves to her mother's pension rather than her own job.
She is honest that distance makes people, including her, procrastinate.

steps.text: Aim for a training contract and keep law grades high
Attend one workshop on how firms use AI tools
Become a student rep with the union branch
Open a small pension pot with the first graduate job

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Steady Disruption worries me most, strangely, because it's the one that's slow enough that nobody acts. What would help is a rule that firms must tell you when a machine made a decision about you, and a union that actually covers young people.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that people assume I'm against technology. I'm not. I'm against being told it's good for me by people who sell it, and I'd like someone neutral to check. Nobody asked my mum and dad if they wanted a future built around machines. They just pay for me to find out whether I'll have one.

headlineQuote: Nobody asked my mum and dad if they wanted a future built around machines. They just pay for me to find out whether I'll have one.
portrait: Maya is 18, a first-year **law** student with top results, sharing a flat while her nurse mother and bus-driver father pay part.
She takes handwritten notes, works at a bookshop and **never uses AI tools**, because she distrusts the companies selling them.
She blames big tech firms and weak regulation, not the technology, and puts her hope in **unions and rules**.
Her mood climbs from uneasy to alarmed as warning time shrinks, driven by **debt** and vanishing trainee jobs.
She is a person who digs in: she would rather organise with other students than adopt a tool she doesn't trust.
biggestWorry: She fears **Steady Disruption** most, because it is slow enough that nobody organises until the entry-level legal jobs have already gone.
whatWouldHelp: She wants a **rule** that firms must disclose machine decisions, and a union that covers young and part-time workers.
